en: Restraining within itself a heart agitated on all sides by intense surges, it generally sustains that root of bliss which consists of ever-new aesthetic relish. Victorious is that certain expansion of consciousness within the heart, which repeatedly obstructs the internal suffering of the dissolution and manifestation [of worldly existence].
Herein, indeed, is the Self of the entire universe—transcending all yet consisting of all—whose nature is the light of consciousness uncontracted by conceptual construction.

The Great Lord, whose nature is consciousness (*saṃvid*), exists as one alone, inlaid with all powers; he rests in uninterrupted consciousness and bliss; he is a great ocean carrying the flowing, dense, and manifold fivefold currents; and he manifests boldly at the limit of unsurpassed sovereignty. His nature as luminosity is the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*); his sovereignty is the power of bliss (*ānandaśakti*); his wonder is the power of will (*icchāśakti*); his essence as reflective awareness is the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*); and his capacity for union with all forms is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).

Thus, although He possesses all powers, that Blessed Lord is designated by these primary powers; and by the majesty of His power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), manifesting Himself as if contracted, He is called an "individual soul" (*aṇu*).
As it has been said: "For Śiva is all-pervasive, yet [He appears limited] due to the seal of contraction fashioned by His own will. (Kārikā 6)
"By the power of a flood of various results of karma, [the Self] assumes this or that body.
(7) Thus, the supreme teachers have understood the vibration of the power of Maheśvara to be intent solely on the playful sport of concealing its own essential nature.
(8) And so they say: "Because of His capacity to accomplish what is exceedingly difficult to achieve, and because of His stainless autonomy... (9)
"The Supreme Lord is skilled in the play of concealing His own nature.

Even though His essential form is unobscured, that which is the Self-concealment of the All-pervasive One is itself ignorance (avidyā), from which arises this entire manifold activity of the universe. (Kārikās 10–12)

And by this much, there is no injury whatsoever to the Blessed One—whose nature consists of the overflowing of unsurpassed bliss, free from the limitations of place, time, and form; on the contrary, there is a further nourishment of His supreme majesty.

For if Maheśvara were to remain with a body of a single, unchanging form, He would have forfeited His status as Maheśvara and His nature as pure Consciousness, just like a jar or other such objects. (14–15)
"Indeed, the defining characteristic of the insentient is that its manifestation is limited.
Since consciousness is distinct from the insentient, it is not measured by limits.
Therefore, its own powers emerge as waves from the great ocean of consciousness. (16–18)

"They assume a variety of forms through their own mutual impact, like waves," and so forth. Thus, this Blessed One, by means of His own power of Māyā— which is the majesty of His unfailing power of absolute freedom (svātantrya)— manifests Himself as if contracted, appearing as the Vijñānākala.
The *pralayākala* and the *sakala* come into being.

Among them, one who is joined with only the single impurity of *āṇava* is called a *vijñānākala*. One who possesses both *āṇava* and *māyīya* is the *apavedya* (unconscious) *pralayākala*. One who possesses all three—*āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārma*—is the *saṃvedya* (conscious); by those very [impurities], he consists of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with *kalā* and ending with *dharaṇī*.

This entire creation of objects exists solely for that purpose. In this regard, the Lord, intent on emission and abiding in the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), agitates *māyā* by means of His powers and creates for the individual soul (*pudgala*) the principle of *kalā*, characterized by limited agency; from that, He also creates what is called limited cognition.

The principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*) is of the nature of some slight desire, and the principle of attachment (*rāgatattva*) is that very state accompanied by attachment; this principle of agency (*kartṛtattva*), being thus possessed of attachment, is divided into three ways according to past, future, and present time—that is the principle of time (*kālatattva*). Furthermore, that which effects the limitation of agency even while attachment remains uniform is the principle of necessity (*niyatitattva*). These constitute the six coverings (*kañcuka*); they exist externally for the individual soul (*pudgala*) who is internally veiled by impurity (*mala*).
And it is said in the system of Cillācakreśvara that Māyā, Kalā, Śuddhavidyā, Rāga, Kāla,
and Niyati are the six coverings (kañcukas) of the limited self due to their nature as veils (āvṛti). And thus, the internal impurity of the individual soul (pudgala) exists like a covering.
"Like husks, there are coverings; therefore, [the soul] is devoid of knowledge and action.

(26) Thus, that *kalā* reveals to the *puruṣa* a limited agency and [manifests] the unmanifest state (*avyaktatva*), which consists of the objects of experience in the form of pleasure, pain, and delusion. (27)

From that, the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*) arises with eightfold qualities; from that, too, the principle of ego (*ahaṃkāratattva*) arises in three divisions—sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa. From the first [sāttvika] ego, the mind (*manas*) is born; from the second [rājasa], the sense organs (*indriyāṇi*); and from the third [tāmasa], the subtle elements (*tanmātrāṇi*). From these, the gross elements (*bhūtāni*) arise. Thus, all this proceeds through the sovereign power of the one primordial God alone.
For one wandering in *saṃsāra* and assuming the state of a limited subject, there is the expansion of the categories (*tattva*). And it has been said:

"The elements, the group of subtle essences (*tanmātra*), the senses, the root [nature], the person (*puruṣa*) joined with the coverings (*kañcuka*), and that which is utterly pure—from *vidyā* up to the power (*śakti*)—this much is the manifold expansion of the waves of the ocean of one's own consciousness. (28–29)
Thus, one should cross over all the waters, having crossed over with the help of the "All-Father" (Saala-utta).
Know yourself as equal to Masi-veṇa.
Thus [it is said]. 30–32.

And it is stated in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* that because there is a variety of perceivers (*pramātṛ*) regarding these aforementioned principles (*tattva*), there arises a variety of objects of perception (*prameya*). For instance: "The principle of Earth (*dharātattva*) is divided according to the distinction between the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) and his power (*śakti*);
together with its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), it should be known as fifteenfold. (33–34)

By this very same method, [the principle] from the *puṃstattva* up to *kalā* is to be known as thirteenfold; the *pralayākala* is like Rudra. Likewise, *māyā* is to be understood [as thirteenfold], while the *jñānakevala* is ninefold.

Likewise, the mantras are of seven kinds, the leaders of the mantras are fivefold, and the lords of the mantra-lords are threefold; Śiva himself is not divided at all. Furthermore, he who knows all these principles (tattvas) according to their true nature— // 38–40 //
That guru is declared to be equal to me, the illuminator of the potency of the mantra.
Men who have been seen, spoken to, or touched by him with a heart of affection are liberated from the sins committed even over seven lifetimes. (41–43)
Thus [ends verse 44].
Therefore, this sequence of principles (tattva-krama) consists of multiple terminations [or levels] (anekāvasāya).
And that uniform form which follows these principles in their respective groups—because it cannot endure being conceived as having a single form—is called *kalā*. [Ends verse 46].
For it is from that [source] that the categories of reality (tattva-varga) cease; thus, that is the power (kalā) called Nivṛtti (Cessation).
And she is established in earth alone.
Because she performs the functions of filling and nourishing in the state of being a cause, she is called the power Pratiṣṭhā (Foundation).

And she (Vidyā) is established pervading [the path] from water up to its root (Prakṛti). (50) When the objects of knowledge are dissolved, due to the predominance of consciousness, there is the power called Vidyā. (51) And she occupies the path beginning with the individual soul (puruṣa) and ending with Māyā. (52)
Because the waves of the sheath have subsided, this is called the digit named Śāntā (the Peaceful).
And that [digit] resides from Śuddhavidyā up to the end of Śakti.
This very group constitutes the fourfold egg, characterized as the earthly, the natural, the māyic, and the śākta.
Because it transcends everything, Śāntyatītā resides within the Śiva-tattva.
(56) Thus [it is said].

However, the supreme reality (tattva), because of its absolute sovereignty, transcends the kalās; yet, the [subordinate] elements of these very kalās are included within it, just as they are within the [higher] tattvas. (57) Thus [it is said].

The worlds (bhuvanas) must also be understood; thus, the object of knowledge (prameya) has been described as having a threefold form—consisting of worlds, principles (tattvas), and kalās—in terms of gross, subtle, and supreme. The means of knowledge (pramāṇa) is likewise threefold, namely as state (pada), mantra, and phoneme (varṇa). Thus, it is said that for the single, full subject (pūrṇapramātṛ), who wanders through transmigratory existence due to his own freedom (svātantrya), there is repose within the sixfold path (ṣaḍvidha-adhvan). // 58 //

And here are the summary verses concerning the conjunction of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the *parigha* [obstacle]: "Nivṛtti consists of one syllable, one mantra, and one phoneme; 'Dharā' (Earth), the sixteen Puruṣas, and 'Agni' (Fire) and 'Nayana' (Eye).

(59) "The other [kalā], Pratiṣṭhā, consists of the phonemes of the principles (*tattva*), 'Agni' (Fire) and 'Nayana' (Eye), the city of the six tastes (*rasa*) and the five arrows (*śara*), and the word of the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*).
(60) "The next kalā, Vidya, consists of the phonemes of the sages (*muni*) and the principles (*tattva*), a mantra of two words, and the world of the eight eyes (*akṣi*). (61)
The reality of the fire-syllable is the single-word mantra and the single world; this is the Fourth (turyā).
(62) The sixteen phonemes are the reality of the word-mantra and the one [world] beyond peace (śāntyatītā).

Thus, having resorted to the atomic mode of existence (*āṇavī vṛtti*), the Blessed One manifests the multitude of beings born from a womb, an egg, moisture, or heat, through various types of birth, lifespan, and experiences.

(65) Therein, the food and drink that has been consumed, by virtue of its digestion, exists in the form of nutritional essence (*rasa*); this comes to rest within the seminal constituent (*śukradhātu*) in the form of blood, flesh, fat, bone, and marrow, and it is there that these progeny are produced. (66)

And so it is stated in the *Sauśruta*: "In this world, of the fourfold food composed of the five elements, endowed with six tastes, and possessing two types or eight types of taste and potency, which is consumed in many ways and has been digested—the subtle essence that is of the nature of *tejas* is called *rasa*. Its seat is the heart, and from the heart, it flows into twenty-four vessels."

Having entered [the body], it nourishes, vitalizes, sustains, and increases the entire body—ten vessels going upwards, ten going downwards, and four going transversely—day after day, by means of karma whose cause is the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). That watery essence (*āpyo rasaḥ*), having reached the liver, spleen, and other organs, acquires coloration. Regarding this, there are indeed verses: 67.1–3. “The essence (*rasa*) that has been described as the first transformation of food is called *rasa* because it pleases (*rasyate*), and it is called *rasa* because it is the source of all fluids (*rasa*). It is called *rasa* because it is the root of all tastes (*rasa*). It is called *rasa* because it is the root of all bodily fluids (*rasa*). It is called *rasa* because it is the root of all strength (*bala*). It is called *rasa* because it is the root of all complexion (*varṇa*). It is called *rasa* because it is the root of all vitality (*ojas*). It is called *rasa* because it is the root of all growth (*vṛddhi*). It is called *rasa* because it is the root of all pleasure (*sukha*). It is called *rasa* because it is the root of all life (*jīvita*). 67.4–5. “That essence (*rasa*) which is produced from the food eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and which is transformed into blood, is called the ‘blood-essence’ (*rakta-rasa*). From that blood-essence, flesh is produced; from flesh, fat; from fat, bone; from bone, marrow; and from marrow, semen. 67.6–8. “The essence (*rasa*) that is produced from the food eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and which is transformed into blood, nourishes the blood-vessels. From blood, flesh is produced; from flesh, fat; from fat, bone; from bone, marrow; and from marrow, semen. This essence (*rasa*) flows through the channels (*srotas*) and, having reached the heart, is distributed throughout the body. 67.9–10. “The essence (*rasa*) that is produced from the food eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and which is transformed into blood, is the root of all bodily constituents (*dhātu*). It is the root of all strength, complexion, and vitality. It is the root of all growth and pleasure. It is the root of all life. 67.11–12. “The essence (*rasa*) that is produced from the food eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and which is transformed into blood, is the root of all bodily functions. It is the root of all mental states. It is the root of all sensory perceptions. It is the root of all volitions. 67.13–14. “The essence (*rasa*) that is produced from the food eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and which is transformed into blood, is the root of all happiness. It is the root of all sorrow. It is the root of all fear. It is the root of all delusion. 67.15–16. “The essence (*rasa*) that is produced from the food eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and which is transformed into blood, is the root of all righteousness (*dharma*). It is the root of all worldly success (*artha*). It is the root of all sensual pleasure (*kāma*). It is the root of all liberation (*mokṣa*). 67.17–18. “The essence (*rasa*) that is produced from the food eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and which is transformed into blood, is the root of all the worlds. It is the root of all the gods. It is the root of all the ancestors. It is the root of all living beings. 67.19–20. “The essence (*rasa*) that is produced from the food eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and which is transformed into blood, is the root of all the Vedas. It is the root of all the sciences (*vidyā*). It is the root of all the arts (*kalā*). It is the root of all the crafts (*śilpa*). 67.21–22. “The essence (*rasa*) that is produced from the food eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and which is transformed into blood, is the root of all the sacrifices (*yajña*). It is the root of all the gifts (*dāna*). It is the root of all the ascetic practices (*tapas*). It is the root of all the vows (*vrata*). 67.23–24. “The essence (*rasa*) that is produced from the food eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and which is transformed into blood, is the root of all the mantras. It is the root of all the incantations (*vidyā*). It is the root of all the spells (*mantra*). It is the root of all the mystical powers (*siddhi*). 67.25–26. “The essence (*rasa*) that is produced from the food eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and which is transformed into blood, is the root of all the stars. It is the root of all the planets. It is the root of all the constellations (*nakṣatra*). It is the root of all the lunar mansions (*tārakā*). 67.27–28. “The essence (*rasa*) that is produced from the food eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and which is transformed into blood, is the root of all the mountains. It is the root of all the rivers. It is the root of all the oceans. It is the root of all the islands. 67.29–30. “The essence (*rasa*) that is produced from the food eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and which is transformed into blood, is the root of all the forests. It is the root of all the trees. It is the root of all the herbs (*oṣadhi*). It is the root of all the creepers (*latā*). 67.31–32. “The essence (*rasa*) that is produced from the food eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and which is transformed into blood, is the root of all the animals. It is the root of all the birds. It is the root of all the insects (*kīṭa*). It is the root of all the creeping creatures (*sarīsṛpa*). 67.33–34. “The essence (*rasa*) that is produced from the food eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and which is transformed into blood, is the root of all the gods. It is the root of all the demons (*asura*). It is the root of all the spirits (*bhūta*). It is the root of all the ghosts (*preta*). 67.35–36. “The essence (*rasa*) that is produced from the food eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and which is transformed into blood, is the root of all the sages (*ṛṣi*). It is the root of all the seers (*muni*). It is the root of all the holy men (*satpuruṣa*). It is the root of all the virtuous ones (*sādhu*). 67.37–38. “The essence (*rasa*) that is produced from the food eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and which is transformed into blood, is the root of all the past. It is the root of all the future. It is the root of all the present. It is the root of all time (*kāla*). 67.39–40. “The essence (*rasa*) that is produced from the food eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and which is transformed into blood, is the root of all existence (*bhava*). It is the root of all non-existence (*abhava*). It is the root of all birth (*janman*). It is the root of all death (*maraṇa*). 67.41–42. “The essence (*rasa*) that is produced from the food eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, and which is transformed into blood, is the root of all happiness. It is the root of all sorrow. It is the root of all fear. It is the root of all delusion. It is the root of all righteousness. It is the root of all worldly success. It is the root of all sensual pleasure. It is the root of all liberation. It is the root of all the worlds. It is the root of all the gods. It is the root of all the ancestors. It is the root of all living beings. It is the root of all the Vedas. It is the root of all the sciences. It is the root of all the arts. It is the root

The waters within the bodies of embodied beings are colored by the vital heat (tejas) residing therein; when they are unimpaired and clear, the wise know that state as "red" (rakta). From that very essence, the menstrual blood known as *rajas* proceeds in women.
By its power, after twelve days, fifty [units] reach the earth.
The menstrual blood is fiery (āgneya) because the embryo partakes of the nature of both Agni and Soma.
From the essence (rasa) comes blood; from that, flesh is born, and from flesh, fat.
From fat comes bone, from that marrow, and from marrow the production of semen.
(74) In this way, through the flesh, the essence gradually attains the state of semen. (75) Likewise, for women, the production of the menstrual flow occurs in one month. (76)

Thus, when it has come to pass that the semen and blood—consisting of fire and moon, produced from the connection between mother and father—immediately after the time of the flower [menstruation], become a *kalala* in the mother's womb; from that, a *budbuda*; from that, a *peśī*; from that, a *ghana*, until the assumption of the limbs.
The manifestation of the limbs, the radiance of consciousness, the perfection of all the limbs, the movement of vital energy (*ojas*), and the perception of pleasure and pain—this is what arises.
Thus it has been stated in the doctrine of the venerable *Cillācakreśvara*: "From the mutual friction of the radiance of the essences of the Moon and the Sun. (78–79)
When Jātavedas has arisen and the central abode has expanded,
the sprout comes into being through the transformation of the hero and the dawn.
Semen that has been emitted and has rested for one night proceeds to the state of the *kalala*.
In seven nights it becomes a bubble, and in one month a fleshy mass (peśī) is produced.

In the second month it becomes a solid mass (ghana), and in the third month there is the acquisition of internal heat (agni). In the fourth month the limbs and their members become distinct, and in the fifth month consciousness (cetanā) arises.
In the sixth month, there is the differentiation of all limbs; in the seventh, movement arises.
In the eighth, heat circulates; in the ninth, sensation occurs.
In the tenth month, the creature is born with a fully developed body.
Once born and touched by the wind, he is crushed by the mechanism of the womb;
he does not remember the intense suffering arising from many previous existences.
Gradually, these causes of his body reach maturity.
Rasa (nutritive essence) establishes stability and thoroughly vitalizes the blood;
it generally increases the flesh and clearly provides moisture to the fat;
likewise, the bones support [the body] by being the refuge for the marrow within their core.
Semen produces an excess of joy; urine effects moisture and separation.
Feces is proclaimed to cause the obstruction of wind and fire. Menstrual blood (ārtava) is the instrument for moisture and sweat, and it is the cause of the womb.
Thus, having obtained a body consisting of six sheaths through its appropriation, a person disregards his own true nature and becomes dependent upon external objects. (98–99) Thus [it is said]. (100)

And this very same meaning was also stated by the author of the *Nirukta*, beginning with the words: "One should know that there are eight qualities of the earthly [elements]: three from the mother and three from the father," and so forth. In this very context, he stated this definition of male, female, and neuter, which has the three *prakṛtis* as its cause: "Through a predominance of *soma* there is birth as a male; through a predominance of *sūrya*, a female; through their equality, a neuter (*klība*); and through the division [of the humors] by wind (*vāta*), there would be many offspring. (101–103)
Thus [it is said]. 104.

Even with its various limbs developed, in the ninth or tenth month, it is expelled by the powerful winds of labor like an arrow through the opening of a machine, while still trembling with distress. 105–106.
Its body is sixfold, and it is supported by six layers of skin. Furthermore, there are three hundred and sixty bones joined together;
including the large ones, there are sixty-four teeth and twenty nails.
There are the phalanges of the hands and feet; in their place, there is a set of four [bones].
There are sixty bones in the fingers and toes, two in the heels, and four in the ankles.
There are four bones in the forearms, and exactly that many in the shanks.

One should point out two each arising from the knees, the cheeks, the pelvic plates, and the shoulders; as well as the sockets of the eyes, the temples, and the two buttocks. There is one bone of the pubic region, and likewise forty-five bones in the back.
The neck consists of fifteen bones, as does each clavicle, and likewise the jaw.
At its base are two [bones], along with the bones of the forehead, eyes, cheeks, nose, and chin.
Together with the ribs and their sockets, there are seventy-two *arbuda* bones.
There are two temples, four skull-bones, and likewise the head;
the chest consists of fifteen bones—such is the collection of bones in a person.
Regarding these very [parts], their designations according to the distinctions of *kapāla*, *bharaṇa*, *turuṇḍa*, *ruṇḍa*, *rucaka*, *nalayaṣṭīla*, and *nalaka* are stated in other treatises.

He states the other locations: "The fat, the *vapā* (omentum), the *vahanana*, the navel, the *kloma*, the liver, the spleen, the small intestines, the *vṛkkaka* (kidneys), the bladder, and the rectum (*purīṣāpāna*). (122–124)
The stomach, the heart, the large intestine, the anus,
and the two upper parts of the anus— this is declared to be the extent of the internal cavity (koṣṭha).
The two pupils, the two eye-sockets, the two ear-wax glands, and the two ear-cavities.
The two cheeks, the two temples, the two eyebrows, the two temples of the head, the two lips, the two *kukundara* cavities;
the two groins, the two testicles, the two kidneys, the two breasts which are a mass of phlegm;
the uvula, the two buttocks, the tongue, the two shanks, the two thighs, and the two calves.
The palate, the interior of the belly, the head of the bladder, the chin, the two tonsils, the four eyelashes, as well as the feet, hands, and heart, and the nape of the neck—
these and others are the locations here in this body. (131–133)
Those very nine apertures are the abodes of the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
there are two hundred vessels (*dhamanī*) and five hundred muscles (*peśī*).
Thus [it is said]. 134–136.

According to Suśruta, there are thirty-eight vessels (dhamanīs) with their respective branches arising from the pits of the breasts of women. There are twenty-nine lakhs and nine hundred ligaments (snāyus). Furthermore, the total number of veins (sirās) and vessels (dhamanīs) should be known as fifty-six thousand.
There are one hundred and seven vital points (marmas), as well as two hundred joints;
there are fifty-four crores of body hairs;
the quantity of rasa is to be known as nine [prasthas], and that of water as ten añjalis.
Seven [palas] are indeed declared for feces, and eight for blood;
six for phlegm, five for bile, and four for urine.
Three for fat, two for muscle-fat, one for marrow, and half a [pala] for the brain.
"Of phlegm-seed (śleṣma-ojas) there is just that much, and of semen there is just that much.
(146) "This body is thus unstable; he who strives for liberation [should realize this].
(147) Thus [it is said] regarding one who is healthy and possesses a balanced constitution. (148)

Otherwise, however, because bodies differ from one another and are in a state of ill-health, there is likewise no fixed measure for the humors (doṣas), constituents (dhātus), and waste products (malas); thus it has been said. 149–151.

This very loathsome vision has been sung by the sages of detachment through its various divisions; and so they have said: "A body with bones for its pillars, bound together by sinews, plastered with flesh and blood, covered with skin, foul-smelling, and filled with urine and excrement;
possessed by old age and sorrow, a dwelling place of disease, and afflicted. (152–154)

A sage should abandon this impermanent abode of the elements, which is characterized by impurity; for even Pārāśarya said: "Fools commit sins for the sake of this very body, which is a repository of all impurities, ungrateful, and perishable. (155-156) How could there be any delight in that which is gradually led toward suffering by means of food? (157)
"For who indeed would perform that which is devoid of Dharma for the sake of the body?
(158) Thus, having spoken of the body, the nature of the embodied self is now described: "Seventy-two thousand [channels] have issued forth from the heart. (160)
There are channels called *hitā* and *ahitā*; in their midst is a mandala with the luster of the moon. Within that, the Self resides, motionless like a lamp.
That is what must be known; having realized it here, one is not born again.
This is the intended meaning here: having known that Self to be such as it is, a person does not experience the affliction of birth.

Of what nature is it? It is that which resides within the wheel of seventy-two thousand channels (nāḍī-cakra) mentioned in the Heart [Sūtra]; within that is the lunar orb, and situated therein are those channels, which are beneficial due to the accumulation of merit because they serve as the conduits for the circulation of the essence of what is eaten and drunk.
In the absence of that [central state], they are unbeneficial; their sole mover is the wind (*vāyu*), which appears as fivefold due to the differentiation of its functions.

Among them, two are primary, connected to the south and the north, and consist of the nature of fire (*agni*) and moon (*soma*). Through those two gates, the upward movement of the *prāṇa* is the day, and the downward movement of the *apāna* is the night. By this, the division of time—consisting of half-months, months, seasons, years, and so forth—is also explained.

The equal flow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the equinox (*viṣuvat*); between those two stands the third, the Brahma-nāḍī, which is shaped like a staff. There, the yogi who has restrained his breath perceives the Self in the form of a lamp. For this very reason it is said: "One endowed with perfect vision is not bound by actions;
but one devoid of vision enters into the cycle of transmigration. (164-165)

Thus [it is said]. And regarding the progression of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), the sages have stated that its differentiation according to objects arises from the constituent parts (*kalā*); for indeed: "Coveting the property of others, likewise brooding over what is undesirable, and being intent on what is false—one is born in the lowest wombs. (167–168)

A man who speaks falsehoods, as well as one who is malicious, and one who indulges in idle chatter, is born among animals and birds. One who is devoted to taking what is not given and one who consorts with another's wife [is likewise reborn there]. 169–171.
"And a violent person is born among stationary beings by way of non-observance of the rules" (verse 172), and so forth.

If it is asked, "Since this is the application of torments for one whose nature is non-dual, from where does this differentiation of the Self arise?", he replies: "It is fashioned by the conceptual constructions of Māyā and great delusion; for just as the single space appears distinct within jars and other vessels. (verse 173)
"Thus, although the Self is one, it appears as many, like the sun reflected in various receptacles of water.

(174) And for one whose passions (*kaṣāya*) have not been matured [or purified], such knowledge of the Self as has been described never occurs; for just as a soiled mirror is incapable of reflecting a form, (176) so too is it with the unpurified mind.
For it has been said: "Thus, one whose faculties are unripened is not capable of self-knowledge" (177), and so forth.
Enough with further elaboration (179).

Thus, that Blessed One, by the majesty of his power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), assuming the state of a bound soul (*paśu*) and intent upon the acquisition of experience, possesses the full strength of body and vital breath; having been awakened by the aforementioned process of the lattice of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhva-jāla-krama*), he sequentially undergoes the assumption of a body. As his karmas are experienced, the bodily machine is subject to the six transformations of being (*bhāva-vikāra*), such as old age, disease, and so forth.

When [the body] begins to disintegrate, there occurs stiffness of the body, trembling, contraction of the network of channels (nāḍīcakra), and in some cases, conversely, their dilation, the breaking of the vital points (marmabhaṅga), emaciation, and so forth; everything that subverts the previous constitution comes to pass until it perishes. And although its destruction is momentary, nevertheless, from a gross perspective, it is said to be manifested through ten [stages] each. // 180 //
For it has been said: "Childhood, growth, strength, wisdom, skin, sight, and hearing—these faculties of men proceed [in decline] by tens [of years] each; [so do] sitting and lying down. (181–183)

And then, when that bodily machine has disintegrated, that consciousness, assuming the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), is led to another body by means of the subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*). Consequently, the subtle body exists as a vehicle between the past and future bodies, mounted upon which this person (*pudgala*) experiences the transition to another body; thus it has been said.
And in the *Kośabhāṣya*: "That which exists here between the state of death and the state of rebirth is the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
Because it is connected to the destination to be reached, the intermediate existence is said to have been 'born' (*upapanna*).
Due to its similarity to the continuity of a grain of rice, its arising is uninterrupted. (184–186)
Because it is not established and because the illustrative example lacks similarity, [the intermediate state] exists between death and the moment of rebirth;
it possesses its own kind, pure sense-faculties, and karma that is visible to those with karmic affinity. (187–189)
Thus [it is said].
And the Śruti says: "O Sūrya, O Brahmāṇas, they know your two wheels according to the seasons;
but that one wheel which is hidden, only those who perceive the truth know it. 191–192.

Thus, this is the meaning: O venerable Sūryā, O divine power of the Self, the knowers of Brahman (brahmavādinaḥ) know your two wheels to be associated with you at each proper time (ṛtuthā). Because of their common property of revolving like a wheel, the body is called a "wheel" (cakra); their duality arises from the distinction between the present and the future. Therefore, that which is [situated] between those two, by the method already stated—

One [of these] is called *ātivāhika*; "hidden in the cave" means it is imperceptible. For this very reason, they know it as "addhātayaḥ"; the purport is that only yogins truly know it. (193) And likewise, in the waking state, for the cognizer who has made his faculties firm, the senses such as hearing and so forth, as well as sounds and so forth—

And likewise, at the time of the object of cognition, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) becomes active as the sense-organ (*indriya*), and the desire to go [toward that object] (*yiyāsutā*) constitutes the object; with reference to that very desire to go, the preeminent sage Pārāśarya [Vyāsa] declared: "Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end... (Gītā 8.6). 194.
"O son of Kuntī, one who is constantly permeated by that state goes to that very [state].

(195) Thus, (196) the summary meaning here is that there are three experiences pertaining to the body: the experience of birth (*sambhava-bhoga*), the experience of existence (*sthiti-bhoga*), and the experience of enjoyment (*bhoga*).
Indeed, there are prior states: for when consciousness has arisen in the womb, there is the experience of the embryo; at the time of birth, the experience of delivery;

and for one who has been born, the diverse experience of remaining through the transitions of ages such as childhood and so forth. There is the experience of death and the desire to depart—these are the two final states. Among these, the experience of death consists of various afflictions of the body, while the desire to depart is connected with the *ātivāhika* (subtle) body; and it is specifically with reference to that very desire to depart [that this is said].
"Whichever state [of being] one remembers...

(198), and so forth, begins from this very point. Therefore, for one who speaks for the benefit of past and future objects, the employment of the word and the cognition "remembering" would be according to its true meaning; and this very point has been explained at length in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* as the experience of death.
This entire [process], which severs the vital points and resides in the sense organs, is characterized by delusion;
therein occurs the confusion of the senses and the state of being overwhelmed by labored breathing.
That which is this single, final moment consisting of the life-force—// 199–201 //
That minute fraction of time at the moment of leaving the body is when one is separated from the vital breaths.
Whatever that [being] remembers at that moment, through the awakening of prior latent impressions,
to that very form it goes, deluded by pleasure, pain, and confusion.
Thus [it is said].
And here, the division according to the restriction of the objects [of rebirth] was made by the sage Vyāsa himself:
"When, however, the embodied soul meets its dissolution while *sattva* has increased... (207).
By such passages as these, [the stages of the body] are described;
they are stated in such Vedic texts as: "These stages of the body abide in that five-spoked wheel which revolves, upon which all worlds rest. (RV 1.164.11). 208–210.
"Elsewhere also, there is the possibility of birth, existence, death, and then the desire to depart.
These five are the transformations and misfortunes of the body.
Thus it has been said.

In this manner, as described, he is led from one body to another by means of the *ātivāhika* (conveying) body; that body, too, having attained awakening like one rising from sleep, breathes through the aforementioned wheel, yet it also perishes. Thus, like the buckets on a waterwheel (*araghaṭṭaghaṭīyantra*), the subtle soul (*aṇu*) revolves and transmigrates through various classes of bodies within the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
And thus says the Śruti: "Like grain, a mortal ripens; like grain, he is born again. (215) And:
"Just as one casts off worn-out clothes... (217)
This has also been stated by the sage Vyāsa with these words [beginning with] "ityādi.

(218) Now, at some point, one who has been purified by the descent of the power of grace (*śaktipāta*) from the Supreme Lord, through some means such as initiation (*dīkṣā*), perceives his own non-dual nature which rests in the bliss of consciousness (*saṃvidānanda*); thereafter, he takes hold of that true nature, as it is said in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*:

Having begun with the words, "Thus, at some time, by virtue of his fitness," and ending with the passage, "At that very moment, or through experience, upon the fall of the body, he shall go to Śiva" (vv.
219–220), [the author] concludes with this section of the text. (v. 221)

Alternatively, having spent one's body in any temple of the Supreme Lord, one gradually becomes the Supreme Goddess through the prior rite; as it is stated in the *Śrīsāttvata*: "Wherever the sound of a conch, proceeding from the gateway of the temple, reaches out in all directions, that place is considered a Vaiṣṇava field. (222–223)
That very same [result] is proclaimed to be twofold when [the mantra] is brought down by a perfected deity (siddha) initiated by a sage; it is remembered as threefold when brought down by a deity;
and for those who have cultivated their selves, it is fourfold at the end of the body when [the mantra] is manifested by itself.
The fruit [of this practice] should be understood as attaining union (sāyujyatā) first, and thereafter [the other goals] in succession.
The mind of men, which has been impelled by defilements due to the power of the wicked senses,
attains complete purification at the time of death in the abode of Nārāyaṇa.

Thus [it is said]. Also, in the venerable *Amṛteśaśikhā*: "But for those who have descended into the principles (*tattva*) and follow the command of Śaṅkara, [the initiation may be performed] in the house of self-arisen beings, sages, celestial seers (*devarṣi*), humans, and so forth. (230–232)
Having died, they reach that city and are consecrated by the lords of the city in due order;
or else, descending into the mortal realm, they proceed to the supreme state by means of a boat. There, the self-existent ones are of two kinds, some of whom are intent upon bestowing grace.
"Some who arrived previously for their own purpose were granted liberation.

(236) Thus it is said: "Even there, not everyone attains liberation; the state of being in the same world (sālokya) belongs to the mere animal-sacrificer, while the state of proximity (sāmīpya) belongs to the initiated. (238)
"But for one who is devoted to that [teaching], there is union (sāyujya); such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
However, he who follows the higher scriptures but has abandoned his faith therein due to doubt—he shall not go to the sacred abode at all and enjoys no fruit whatsoever. (239–241)
But those who, with their minds, harbor hatred toward the knowledge of the seats of initiation (dīkṣāyatana),
and yet practice it— they indeed all go to hell.
However, those whose very nature consists of well-practiced knowledge are indeed identical with Śiva.
"For those who are liberated while living (jīvanmukta), there is no further deliberation whatsoever regarding death.
Thus [it is said].
For this very reason, it is stated in the venerable Niśāṭana: "Whether it be the milking of a cow, the flight of an arrow, or the opening of an eye... [247]
One who is correctly united with the supreme reality shall not undergo birth again.
(248) Since he has previously himself placed his own self into Brahman, the supreme, (249) how can there be any recollection for him when the end of life has arrived? (250)
Thus [it is said]. 251.
Even in the case of the venerable Śrī Rāmabhaṭṭāraka, the field and the sacred site (tīrtha) exist only so long as one has not entered into Brahman. 252.
Having known that, even a dog-cooker (śvapāka) is equal to me; there is no doubt in this matter. 253.
Thus [it is said].

Even by the Blessed One, the Lord of Beings, whether at a sacred ford or in the house of an outcaste, even if he has lost his memory while casting off the body, he is liberated simultaneously with the arising of knowledge; with his sorrows destroyed, he attains absolute isolation (*kaivalya*).

Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the venerable *Pauṣkara*, it is stated: "Established as a deity among the principles (tattvas) ending with the earth-element, he is a knower of mantras, a devotee of the Lord, full of faith, and ever-orthodox."
In whichever stage of life he may dwell, with his senses restrained,

he should constantly remember his own mantra situated within his own body, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon his form. At the time of renouncing the body, wherever he may find rest, [he should remain there].
"He indeed proceeds to the primordial state, having transcended his own body.
Thus [it is said]. Elsewhere also: "The body alone is the abode; one does not go to any other abode. 265.
"One should resort to a single sacred mantra and avoid other sacred sites," [so it is said].
Likewise, O Nārada, those mortals who remember me while their faculties are healthy and active—I remember them at the time of death as being equal to wood or stone. (266–268)
Thus it has been said.

Furthermore, for one who is established in the highest state and is thus qualified, lamentation such as the shedding of tears—which is well known in worldly conduct—must not be performed; as stated in the *Śrīpūrvaśāsana*, weeping is prohibited in all scriptures as a mere instruction for the body.
"Specifically in the Bhairava Tantra, the Śambara [rite] is conceived as a sacrificial animal (paśu).
One should indeed abandon this improper practice, for it does not lead to the state beyond this life.
Thus [it is said]. (271–273)

In the *Śrīmatarahasyatilaka* as well, it is taught that for those qualified by the supreme method (*uttamanaya*) who maintain their own secret conduct, they must not abandon that conduct in order to protect their reputation in the world; for it is said: "The worldly custom must never be interrupted;
[the practice] should be kept secret, even more secret, external, and likewise both external and internal. (vv. 274–275)

Regarding these two positions, the preeminent gurus alone are the authority for adhering to either one. Furthermore, it has been stated in the *Śrīmahākula*—which is composed in aphoristic style (*sūtra*), though its divisions are somewhat obscured—that sacrifices, recitations, burnt offerings, fasts, and so forth, dedicated to the father, must certainly be performed after propitiating the guru, even if one does not summon the mantra within the mandala as prescribed by the ritual rules, provided that [the site] possesses the desired lunar days. 276–278.
The seventy million mantras bring their presence;
how much more so the Kaulika tradition when it is invoked and worshipped there? O auspicious lady, when dedicated to the ancestors, it leads to infinity.
Thus it is said.

Furthermore, in the *Śrīpracaṇḍabhairava* it is stated: "Those mortals who possess little wealth, though devoted to their guru and mantra, are especially incapable of performing the worship of the Great Sacrifice. (282–284)
Then, for the sake of their ancestors, the wise man should worship that Siddhaliṅga;
there, the appropriate worship is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
There, he uplifts ten generations of his lineage, both preceding and following him.
Thus [it is said]. 288.
Also in the Śrībhāgeśamata: "By poison, snakes, fire, epilepsy, hunger, overeating, and imprisonment; 289.
by outcastes, water, thunderbolts, royal edicts, and thieves; 290."
By those who dwelt in great herds of cattle scorched by the summer heat and trapped in carts,
and by those who followed the terrifying methods of uprooting Brahmins, Mlecchas, and heretics—
those of evil deeds who were slain, and those who were devoted to betraying their friends.
O woman of excellent complexion, for those who have committed treason against their master, others who have likewise harmed themselves,
pregnant women of ill-repute, and those who have died during childbirth—
there is no other means of deliverance for them.
"Without sacrifice, without fire-offering, without the formal assumption of a physical form;
without the application of the procedure of the Great Net (mahājāla) for extracting the individual soul (pudgala);
[this is] the initiation known as the 'Extraction of the Dead' (mṛtoddharaṇa), which pertains to all levels of the cosmic path. (297–299)
Thus, this is first the procedure for those who abide by the higher teaching.
For others, however, the performance of practices prescribed in their own scriptures and traditions is indeed superior; so, enough of this.

In this manner, having ascertained the connection to the continuous chain of birth and death through the principle just described, and having attained liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) by means of the contemplation of one's own uncreated nature, they take hold of the state of having accomplished all that was to be done.

O peaceful ones! As it has been said: "The gods, having understood the true nature of consciousness, [should drink] that which arises from the churning and extraction by the strength of the immovable heart from the ocean of consciousness. If they swallow what is called 'nectar' even when the Kālakūṭa poison is present, then at that time your state of Śiva-hood is certain. (302–304)
Thus [ends the verse].
Vāmadeva, having attained his state through the grace of the illustrious teacher Yogeśvara,
composed this investigation into birth and death.
The women slow with fresh passion, the sweet compositions of songs in the season of spring—alas, alas!
these words, with their graceful syllables and pregnant with secret matters, steal away my heart.
This is the work of the venerable and illustrious Bhaṭṭa Vāmadeva, the preeminent teacher and great devotee of Maheśvara.
When the assembly of texts and scholars who were the refuge of the six sciences had undergone decline due to the passage of time (311),

the illustrious sovereign of Kaśmīra— whose strength lay in his noble discernment and whose sole intent was the desire to uphold those various True Dharmas— for the sake of [reviving] their activity, deliberated together with his chief ministers who were devoted to the Dharma (312–313).

He established the headquarters for the purpose of extracting the core texts from the *Jñānavijñānagarbha*. May this work, refined through completion, purification, and commentary by virtuous men who lived there under the supervision of Mukundarāma until their lives' end, be for the spiritual welfare of the righteous. (314–316)
The Tilaka: 317.
May this [offering] be dedicated to Śaṅkara, whose body is the nectar of the consciousness of one’s own glorious Self. 318.
